question:
Please answer this question with a number--which of the following best apply to the design in the study: 
        (1) totally fun first (i.e., Entertainment game reappropriated), 
        (2) mostly fun first (i.e., design workshop with disabled stakeholders),
        (3) both fun and utility first (i.e., design workshop with diverse stakeholders), 
        (4) mostly utility first (i.e., primary utilitarian mechanic designed first),
        (5) totally utility first (i.e., made by clinicians or specialists, fun incorporated later)
reasoning: The system is an assistive AAC/narrative tool built around data-to-text NLG, sensor data, and VOCA integration, with extensive information gathering from therapists, teachers, parents, and ethnographic study to ensure it fits the school environment. The focus is on supporting personal narrative and communication for children with severe speech and physical impairments, not on entertainment or games. Design is user-centred with school staff and students involved, but there is no indication of entertainment or game-like fun as a primary goal; the primary mechanic is utilitarian (AAC narrative support) designed first, with usability and engagement considered within that frame. This aligns best with a mostly utility-first design (4), not clinician-only (5) because HCI researchers and diverse school stakeholders are involved rather than only clinicians, and not fun-first options (1–3) since no entertainment/game framing is described.

question:
Please answer this question with a number--which of the following best apply to the design in the study: 
        (1) unstructured play (i.e., no rules, making art),
        (2) semi-structured play (i.e., playground activities),
        (3) flexible structure with rules (i.e., improv),
        (4) flexible game (i.e., board game with house rules),
        (5) game with rigid rules (i.e., video game)
reasoning: The study centers on a mobile phone and VOCA-based assistive technology with defined interaction mechanics (recording, storing, and playing back sequenced voice messages, switch activation, automatic data transfer, server-side narrative generation). These are structured, rule-governed interactions more akin to a rigid system than open or loosely structured play. There is no indication of house rules or improvisational rule-bending; instead, children follow fixed device operations to access narratives, best matching a game/system with rigid rules.

question:
Please answer this question with a number--which of the following best apply to the design in the study: 
        (1) entirely skill-based (i.e., trivia, sports),
        (2) mostly skill-based (i.e., mario kart),
        (3) equally skill and chance-based (i.e., catan),
        (4) mostly chance-based (i.e., Uno),
        (5) entirely chance-based (i.e., all dice)
reasoning: The study is not a game but an assistive narrative tool where staff and children record and play back voice messages, take photos, and use tagged objects/locations. Outcomes depend entirely on users’ communicative and operational skills with the device; there is no randomization or chance mechanic. This best matches an entirely skill-based design.

question:
Please answer this question with a number--which of the following best apply to the design in the study: 
        (1) entirely solo (i.e., solitaire),
        (2) mostly solo (i.e., playing against AI in single-player StarCraft),
        (3) mix of solo and social affordances (i.e., animal crossing),
        (4) mostly social, but aspects are independent (i.e., house on hill haunt transition),
        (5) entirely social (i.e., tag)
reasoning: The system is designed for children to tell and share personal narratives with adults and peers, supporting interactive conversation and social dialogue, but each child independently plays back and controls their own device. This indicates a mix of solo interaction with strong social affordances rather than being purely solo or entirely social.

question:
Please answer this question with a number--which of the following best apply to the design in the study: 
        (1) entirely turn-based (i.e., tic tac toe),
        (2) follows a set of steps (i.e., viticulture's dynamic turn ordering),
        (3) turns are taken, but some actions can be taken at any time (i.e., pandemic),
        (4) most actions can be taken at any time, but there are some phases (i.e., PvP death reset timer),
        (5) entirely simultaneous (i.e., race)
reasoning: The system supports interactive narrative where children play back pre-recorded voice messages and show photos during conversations. There is no strict turn structure like a game; instead, actions (recording, playback, showing photos) are taken as needed within conversational flow, implying turns exist in conversation but actions (e.g., playing a message) can be taken at various times. This best matches a design where turns are taken but some actions can occur at any time.

question:
Please answer this question with a number--which of the following best apply to the design in the study: 
        (1) entirely synchronous (i.e., real time strategy game),
        (2) mostly synchronous with a few asynchronous affordances (i.e., league of legends),
        (3) equal mix of synchronous and asynchronous affordances (i.e., helldivers 2),
        (4) mostly asynchronous with few synchronous affordances (i.e. cookie clicker),
        (5) entirely asynchronous (i.e., chess by postage mail)
reasoning: The system supports recording events during the day and later playback of stored voice messages and photos for narrative sharing. Interaction is based on pre-recorded sequences and later retrieval, not real-time multi-user coordination. This is best characterized as entirely asynchronous.

question:
Please answer this question with a number--which of the following best apply to the design in the study: 
        (1) entirely competitive (i.e., spit card game),
        (2) mostly competitive, but sometimes collaboration is important (i.e., forbidden island),
        (3) mix of competitive and collaborative (i.e., mario party 2 vs 2 mini-games),
        (4) mostly collaborative (i.e., animal crossing),
        (5) entirely collaborative (i.e., pandemic)
reasoning: The system is an assistive AAC/narrative tool used by children, staff, and parents to support personal narrative and social dialogue. There is no game-like or competitive mechanic; interactions are about sharing stories and communication support. This is entirely collaborative in nature.

question:
Please answer this question with a number--which of the following best apply to the design in the study: 
        (1) entirely symmetrical (i.e., tic tac toe),
        (2) mostly symmetrical (i.e., undertale's differing NPC behaviors based on previous playthroughs),
        (3) both symmetrical and asymmetrical (i.e., pandemic with its similar turn structure but different character abilities),
        (4) mostly asymmetrical (i.e., tag),
        (5) entirely asymmetrical (i.e., keep talking, nobody explodes)
reasoning: The system supports narrative sharing between a child with severe speech and physical impairments and communication partners (staff, parents, peers). Roles and capabilities are fundamentally different: staff record and structure messages, operate parts of the system, and the child primarily plays back and shares narratives via assistive access methods. This strong role and capability differentiation makes the interaction structure entirely asymmetrical rather than turn-symmetric like a standard game.
